rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi},\qquad \Delta x\cdot\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$$
$$\Delta E\cdot\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi},\qquad \Delta L\cdot\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$$
$$\Delta p=m\Delta v,\qquad KE=\frac{(\Delta p)^{2}}{2m}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ The principle is due to clumsy instruments. ✅ It is fundamental; better instruments cannot beat h/4π.  ·  ❌ It says nothing about the electron can be known. ✅ Either quantity may be exact; only the *product* of uncertainties is bounded below.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Heisenberg published the principle in 1927 and received the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics.  ·  ħ = h/2π = 1.054 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; the bound is often written Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Minimum velocity uncertainty for an electron localised within 10⁻¹⁰ m. **Solution:** Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ — comparable to the electron's own speed, so the orbit picture collapses.  ·  **Problem:** Can an electron be confined in a nucleus of radius 10⁻¹⁵ m? **Solution:** Δp ≈ h/(4πΔx) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁰ kg m s⁻¹ → KE ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 10¹⁰ eV, far beyond nuclear binding energies; β-particles are therefore created during decay, not stored in the nucleus.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: heisenberg's uncertainty principle, concept of probability (within Atomic Structure).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning and statement  ·  Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed that for a microscopic particle it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both its position and its momentum: $\Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or $\Delta x\cdot\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$. Other conjugate pairs obey the same pattern: $\Delta E\cdot\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ and $\Delta L\cdot\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: The most probable distance of the 1s electron is 0.529 Å — the value Bohr called the first-orbit radius.  ·  P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Write both forms: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π and Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm — questions often ask about velocity.  ·  Use the principle to justify atomic size (~10⁻¹⁰ m) and stability; these are standard 3-mark applications.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle  ·  • Concept of probability

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Multiplicative: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A); independence: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).  ·  Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A). For discrete: ΣP = 1; expected value E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Worked: identify given → pick sub-concept → apply standard form → check units / edges.  ·  **Problem:** Δx = 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m for an electron — find Δv. **Solution:** Δv = h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 5×10⁻¹¹) ≈ 1.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ — over half the orbital speed, confirming the orbit picture's collapse.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Why it happens  ·  To locate an electron we must 'illuminate' it with radiation of wavelength comparable to its size; such a photon collides with the electron and changes its momentum by an unknown amount, while using longer-wavelength radiation blurs the position. The disturbance is a property of matter, not an experimental defect — the γ-ray microscope is the standard illustration.  ·  ### 3. Consequence: the concept of probability

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)  ·  P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A)  ·  P(A') = 1 − P(A)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi};\quad \Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi};\quad \Delta L\,\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$$  ·  $$KE\approx\frac{(\Delta p)^{2}}{2m}$$  ·  ❌ It applies equally to a moving cricket ball. ✅ For macroscopic bodies the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical physics applies.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The principle proves electrons do not exist in atoms. ✅ It replaces fixed orbits by probability distributions (orbitals) described by |ψ|².  ·  ❌ ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π is a different law. ✅ It is the energy–time form of the same principle, explaining natural line broadening.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ p(e) = favourable/total. additive law: p(a∪b) = p(a)+p(b)−p(a∩b). if mutually exclusive, p(a∪b)=p(a)+p(b)..

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The principle sets a limit on *both* quantities individually. ✅ Only the *product* of the two uncertainties is bounded; either one alone can be exact.  ·  ❌ ΔE·Δt means energy conservation is violated. ✅ It permits transient fluctuations within ΔE for times shorter than Δt — the basis of virtual processes and tunnelling.  ·  ❌ A better microscope can beat the limit. ✅ The limit is fundamental, not technical.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State clearly that the limit is fundamental, not instrumental.  ·  Write the form the question asks for (momentum or velocity); mixing m into the denominator wrongly is the common error.  ·  Conclude numericals with the physical meaning (no definite orbit / no electron in the nucleus).
